d: Hypothetical route: archaic humans often called Homo heidelbergensis carried Late Acheulean handaxes into Europe from about 700,000 years ago, and occupation became frequent after 500,000 years ago (Boxgrove, England, ~500,000 years). The ~430,000-year-old Sima de los Huesos people in Spain already belong to the Neanderthal line.

n: Early modern-human gene flow into Neanderthals
w: Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans
d: Hypothetical route, inferred only from genetics: an early population related to Homo sapiens left Africa and interbred with Neanderthal ancestors between about 370,000 and 250,000 years ago, replacing the Neanderthal Y chromosome (and probably mitochondrial DNA). No fossils show where this happened.

Hypothetical route: fossils with early modern features appear across Africa by about 315,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud, Morocco), 260,000 (Florisbad, South Africa) and 233,000 (Omo, Ethiopia). Many researchers now think Homo sapiens emerged from linked populations across the continent rather than in one place.

Hypothetical route: a partial skull (Apidima 1) from Apidima Cave in southern Greece, dated to over 210,000 years ago, has been identified as an early Homo sapiens; this is contested, and others see an archaic form. If correct, the group was later replaced by Neanderthals (Apidima 2, over 170,000 years).

Hypothetical route (direction unknown): Denisovans, known from the Altai's Denisova Cave from about 200,000 years ago, were on the Tibetan Plateau by 160,000 years ago (Xiahe jaw, Baishiya Karst Cave, 3,280 m), and sediment DNA shows them there until at least 60,000 years ago. Their EPAS1 gene variant helps Tibetans live at altitude today.

n: Denisovans across East and Southeast Asia
d: Hypothetical route: Denisovan fossils identified by DNA or proteins come from Laos (Tam Ngu Hao 2 tooth, about 164,000–131,000 years ago), Harbin in Manchuria (skull, at least 146,000 years) and the seabed of the Penghu channel off Taiwan, showing a range across much of East Asia; how they moved between these places is unknown.

n: Early modern humans into the Levant (Misliya)
d: Hypothetical route: an upper jaw from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, Israel, dated to 194,000–177,000 years ago, is one of the oldest Homo sapiens fossils outside Africa, suggesting modern humans moved in and out of the Levant several times.

Hypothetical route: stone tools at Jebel Faya (UAE) dated to about 125,000 years ago resemble East African tools, suggesting modern humans crossed into Arabia when monsoon rains turned its deserts green; the crossing point (Bab-el-Mandeb or Sinai) is debated and the oldest Arabian human fossil is later, about 85,000 years.

Hypothetical route: modern humans buried their dead at Skhul and Qafzeh caves in Israel about 120,000–90,000 years ago, when the Last Interglacial greened the Sahara and Sinai; this early group did not last, and Neanderthals later reoccupied the region.

Hypothetical route: Neanderthals visited Denisova Cave in the Altai by about 190,000 and 100,000 years ago; the genome of the Chagyrskaya Neanderthal (about 80,000–60,000 years ago) is closer to Croatian Neanderthals than to the older Altai Neanderthal, showing that western Neanderthals spread east and replaced earlier Siberian groups.

n: Early modern humans in southern China? (Fuyan)
d: Hypothetical and contested: 47 modern-looking human teeth from Fuyan Cave, Hunan, were dated to 120,000–80,000 years ago, implying a very early arrival in China; a later ancient-DNA study argues the teeth are Holocene, so this early wave remains in doubt.

Hypothetical route: Middle Palaeolithic tools at Jwalapuram in southern India, from both before and after the Toba eruption about 74,000 years ago, have been attributed to early modern humans arriving from Arabia; no human fossils were found, so archaic makers are equally possible.

n: Neanderthals into the Levant and Zagros
d: Hypothetical route: after the Skhul–Qafzeh modern humans disappeared, Neanderthals occupied the Levant and Zagros (Kebara and Amud in Israel, Shanidar in Iraq, roughly 70,000–50,000 years ago; est.), probably moving south from Anatolia in colder phases. Neanderthals had used the region earlier too (Tabun Cave, perhaps ~120,000 years).
Small groups of modern humans left East Africa across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait about 70,000–50,000 years ago, spreading along the coasts of Arabia and Persia to South and Southeast Asia.
vol: a few thousand at most (genetic estimates of the founding group, 1,000–10,000; est.)

d: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians island-hopped from Southeast Asia to Sahul about 65,000–50,000 years ago, via Timor to the Kimberley or via the Moluccas to New Guinea, reaching Lake Mungo by 41,000 years ago.
vol: at least 1,300–1,550 founders (Bradshaw et al. 2019; est.)

n: First Homo sapiens wave into Europe (Mandrin)
d: Hypothetical route: a modern human tooth and Neronian points at Grotte Mandrin in France's Rhône valley date to about 54,000 years ago, roughly 10,000 years before the main wave; this group, probably from the Levant, apparently vanished and Neanderthals returned to the cave.

n: Denisovan ancestry into Papuans and Australians
d: Hypothetical route: Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and the Aeta of the Philippines carry up to about 5% Denisovan DNA, from interbreeding after about 50,000 years ago and before Papuans and Australians split ~37,000 years ago, probably in Wallacea or Sundaland; the arrow marks a likely meeting zone, not a known route.
Modern humans spread from Southeast Asia into China (Tianyuan Man ~40,000 years ago), Korea, Japan and Siberia by about 35,000 years ago, reaching the Arctic Yana River by about 32,000 years ago.

Modern humans expanding from a Persian-plateau hub 48,000–46,000 years ago entered Europe via the Levant and Balkans, reaching Germany, Italy and Britain by ~44,000 years ago; Aurignacian culture followed.

As glaciers retreated after ~20,000 years ago, Magdalenian peoples from southwestern refugia recolonised Western and Central Europe, while Epigravettian groups from Italy spread east toward the East European Plain.
A small founding population from Beringia moved south along the deglaciated Pacific coast (the 'kelp highway') from about 16,000 years ago, before the interior corridor opened.
vol: a few hundred to a few thousand founders (genetic estimates; est., contested)

d: Paleo-Indians moved through Central America down the Pacific side of South America, reaching Monte Verde in southern Chile by about 14,500 years ago.
An inland route between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets opened about 13,800 years ago, linking Beringia to the Great Plains, where the Clovis culture appears about 13,000 years ago.
Farmers from western Anatolia brought agriculture to Greece by c. 6500 BC (Knossos, Thessaly), then spread north into the Balkans, largely by demic diffusion of Near Eastern farmers.
Seafaring farmers planted coastal colonies from Epirus and Corfu along the Adriatic, Italy, southern France and Iberia to Portugal and Morocco, about 2,000 km in 100–200 years.
Sheep, goats, wheat and barley, perhaps with Fertile Crescent migrants, reached Egypt from the Levant via Sinai around 6000 BC, founding Faiyum A and Merimde farming cultures.
Linear Pottery farmers spread from the middle Danube across Central Europe, from the Paris Basin to the Dnieper, c. 5500–4500 BC; whether by migration or local adoption is debated.
Neolithic farmers of Iberian-related ancestry arrived by mass migration around 4100–4000 BC, almost completely replacing Britain's and Ireland's Mesolithic hunter-gatherers.

Bantu-speaking farmers spread from the Cameroon–Nigeria highlands c. 4000 BC–500 AD: a western stream through the Congo rainforest to Angola, an eastern stream via the Great Lakes to KwaZulu-Natal by 300 AD.

Steppe herders of the pre-Yamnaya Repin culture moved east across the steppe from the Don–Volga to the Altai and Minusinsk Basin, founding the Afanasievo culture; possible ancestors of the Tocharians.

n: Austronesian expansion (Taiwan to Island SE Asia)
d: Austronesian seafarers from Taiwan reached the Batanes by c. 2200 BCE, then spread through the Philippines, Borneo and Indonesia and across to the Marianas by 1500 BCE.
A massive migration from the Pontic–Caspian steppe carried Yamnaya-related ancestry into Central and Northern Europe, forming the Corded Ware culture from the Rhine to the Volga and into Scandinavia.
Rice farming spread from the Yangtze to Lingnan and Fujian (2500–2000 BC), then with Austroasiatic and Kra–Dai migrants into Thailand and Vietnam (Ban Chiang, An Sơn, 2000–1200 BC).

Indo-Aryan speakers from the Sintashta–Andronovo steppe moved south via the BMAC oasis and Hindu Kush into the Punjab c. 2000–1500 BCE and later the Ganges plain, with a branch reaching Mitanni in Syria.

Lapita seafarers, descended from northern Philippine migrants, spread from the Bismarck Archipelago (1600–1200 BCE) through the Solomons, Vanuatu and New Caledonia to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by c. 1000 BCE.

Seafaring confederations, likely from the Aegean, western Anatolia and the central Mediterranean, raided Hatti, Ugarit, Cyprus and Egypt c. 1200 BC; Philistines and others then settled coastal Canaan.
From the late 10th century BC, Tyrian merchants founded trading colonies across the Mediterranean in Cyprus, Sicily, Sardinia, Malta, North Africa and Iberia, including Carthage (814 BC).
Driven by land scarcity, drought, exile and trade, about twenty Greek city-states founded hundreds of colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea, from Massalia to Sinope and Cyrene, 750–500 BC.
La Tène Celts poured through the Alpine passes into Italy (sacking Rome, 390 BC) and down the Danube into the Balkans, Thrace and central Anatolia (Galatia), reaching their greatest extent by 275 BC.

Rice-farming migrants, primarily from the Korean peninsula, crossed to the Japanese archipelago in the Yayoi period, spreading agriculture and Japonic languages and largely absorbing the Jōmon population (~75,000).
vol: up to about 1 million over a thousand years in one model (Hanihara 1987; contested, others argue far fewer)

d: Nomadic Huns from Central Asia crossed the Volga around 370, driving Goths and Alans west, settled the Hungarian Plain and under Attila invaded Gaul (451) and Italy (452) before collapsing c. 454.

Fleeing the Huns, 90,000–200,000 Goths crossed the Danube in 376, moved through the Balkans, sacked Rome in 410, settled in Gaul (the Visigothic Kingdom of Toulouse, 418) and expanded into Iberia from 456.
Austronesian voyagers from Island Southeast Asia crossed the Indian Ocean to settle Madagascar, estimated between the 5th and 7th centuries CE.
After Roman rule ended, Angles, Saxons and Jutes from northwestern Germany, Jutland and Frisia—20,000 to 200,000 people—settled eastern and southern Britain, especially East Anglia, Kent and Wessex.
Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine in 405/406, crossed the Pyrenees into Iberia (409) and, under Genseric, about 80,000 people crossed to Africa (429), seizing Carthage in 439.
vol: about 80,000 crossed to Africa in 429 (ancient figure)

d: Lombards moved from the upper Oder to Rugiland and Pannonia, then in 568 Alboin led some 150,000 people, including 20,000 Saxon warriors, into Italy, taking Pavia in 572.

Slavs from the Polesia region between Vistula and Dnieper spread south into the Balkans, west to the Elbe and east toward the Volga in the 6th–8th centuries, making eastern Europe largely Slavic-speaking.
The Romani, originating in northern India, migrated northwest through Persia (6th c.), Armenia (8th c.) and Byzantine Anatolia into the Balkans from the 9th century and Western Europe in the 15th.

Turkic tribes from Mongolia and the Altai spread across the Eurasian steppe in the 6th–11th centuries; Oghuz and Seljuq Turks reached Iran and Anatolia, while Pechenegs and Cumans pushed toward the Danube.

Arab armies, followed by large-scale migration of families and whole tribes, spread from Arabia across Syria, Iraq, Persia, Egypt, the Maghreb, Iberia (711), Transoxiana and Sindh between 622 and 750.
After a long pause in Samoa and Tonga, Polynesians resumed eastward voyaging around 700 AD, settling the Cook Islands, French Polynesia and the Marquesas.
Polynesian voyagers from East Polynesia sailed north across the equator to settle the Hawaiian Islands by 900 AD.
Polynesians from French Polynesia voyaged east via the Tuamotus and Mangareva to settle remote Rapa Nui (Easter Island) by 1000 AD.
Polynesian voyagers from East Polynesia sailed south-west via the Kermadecs to settle New Zealand (Aotearoa) by about 1250–1300 AD, the last major landmass to be settled.
vol: a few hundred founders (mtDNA estimate; est.)

n: Viking raids and settlement in the West
d: Scandinavian raiders from Lindisfarne (793) onward turned to settlement: the Great Heathen Army founded the Danelaw (876), Norse kings ruled Dublin, and Rollo's Danes received Normandy (911).

Swedish Varangians migrated along the rivers of Russia, Belarus and Ukraine in the 9th–10th centuries, founding the Rurik dynasty of Kievan Rus' and trading and raiding to Constantinople and the Caspian.

n: Norse settlement of the North Atlantic
d: Norse settlers from Norway colonised the Faroes, Iceland (c. 870–874) and southwest Greenland (c. 986), and briefly reached Vinland at L'Anse aux Meadows, dated to 1021.

n: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin
w: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin
d: Driven west, most likely by a joint Pecheneg–Bulgarian attack, Magyars from Etelköz on the Pontic steppe crossed the Carpathians in 894/895 and conquered the Basin by 907.
Ancestors of the Inuit moved from the Bering Strait across Arctic Canada to Greenland, following bowhead whales in the medieval warm period and displacing the Dorset culture by c. 1300.
Mongol armies from the steppe conquered from China (Song falling in 1279) to Rus' (1237–40) and the Middle East, killing an estimated 20–60 million; halted by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut (1260).
From 1492 Spain, and from 1500 Portugal, colonised the Caribbean, Mexico, Peru and Brazil; perhaps 240,000 Europeans arrived in the 16th century while the Indigenous population fell by about 80–90%.
About 12.75 million enslaved Africans were shipped, mainly from West Central Africa and the Bight of Benin, to Brazil, the Caribbean and the Americas; about 10.7 million survived the crossing.
Starting with some 540 Cossacks under Yermak, Russians advanced east along the Ob, Yenisei and Lena rivers, founding Tobolsk (1587) and Yakutsk (1632) and reaching the Pacific by 1639.

n: English and French colonisation of North America
d: English settlers founded Jamestown (1607), largely peopled by indentured servants, and French colonists Quebec (1608); New France grew from about 3,000 settlers in 1663 to some 65,000 by 1760.
About 20,000 Puritans, mainly from East Anglia and Lincolnshire, emigrated to Massachusetts Bay seeking freedom to practise their faith amid religious and political conflict under Charles I.
About 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw were forcibly removed from the Southeastern US to Indian Territory (Oklahoma) after the 1830 Indian Removal Act; 13,200–16,700 died.
More than 1.6 million Indian indentured labourers shipped from Calcutta and Madras to plantations in Mauritius, British Guiana, Trinidad, Natal, Fiji and Suriname between 1834 and 1917.

n: European mass emigration to the United States
d: Over 30 million Europeans, first from Germany, Ireland and Scandinavia, after 1890 mainly from Italy and Eastern Europe, emigrated to the United States between 1836 and 1914, peaking at 1.29 million in 1907.
Fleeing the potato famine, at least 2.1 million people left Ireland in 1845–1855, about a million to North America and 200,000+ to Britain; one in five sailing to Canada in 1847 died.

Millions of labourers from Guangdong and Fujian left via treaty ports and Hong Kong for Malaya, Singapore, the Caribbean and California's gold fields; by 1957 an estimated 8.2 million overseas Chinese traced their origin to Guangdong.
vol: about 19 million Chinese emigrants 1846–1940, mostly to Southeast Asia (McKeown 2004; est.)

d: Millions of Europeans, chiefly 3.8 million Italians and 1.5 million Spaniards between 1861 and 1920, settled in Argentina, mostly arriving through the port of Buenos Aires.
